1142.title: The Book of Knowledge
1142.hook: the first book: foundations, character, study, idolatry and repentance
1142.howItsDone: Jews who study the Mishneh Torah often begin with the Book of Knowledge, and some study a set portion of the code each day, working through it in order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishneh Torah, Maimonides' great code, and your line: the whole law in order. Today, the book that opens it.

A law code is a practical thing. You open it with a question in hand: may I carry this on Shabbat, is this pot still kosher, what do I owe the worker by sundown. So you might expect Maimonides' code to start with something useful. A blessing over bread. The rules of the morning. Instead, its first book is about what a person knows. Who God is. What a good character looks like. Why study matters. What it means to worship something false. How to come back after doing wrong. Only after all that does the code turn to prayer, Shabbat and food.
screen: `A CODE FOR PRACTICAL QUESTIONS.` → `IT DOESN'T START WITH BREAD.` → `IT STARTS WITH KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Sefer HaMadda. Sefer is book, madda is knowledge: the Book of Knowledge. First, what's inside. Maimonides groups his code into books, and each book into sets of laws. This one holds the laws of the foundations of the Torah, of character, of Torah study, of idolatry, and of repentance. Notice the path that list walks. Knowing God. Becoming a certain kind of person. Learning. Guarding against false worship. Returning when you fall. Second, the surprise. These are laws. He writes about knowing God and shaping your temper in the same plain, orderly style he uses elsewhere for damages and contracts. To him, how you think and who you are fall under commandment as much as what you eat. Third, the order. He could have put this book anywhere. He put it first. The inner life comes first, and the outward life of blessings, festivals and courts is built on top of it. Knowing comes before doing. Fourth, the last word. The book ends with repentance, teshuvah. Before the reader meets a single rule about Shabbat or food, the code has already explained how to come back from failing. Knowledge first, and a way home already built in.
screen: `BOOK. KNOWLEDGE. THE BOOK OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `INNER LIFE, WRITTEN AS LAW.` · `HE PUT IT FIRST.` · `IT ENDS WITH RETURN.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here is the code's first line, in plain English: the foundation of foundations, and the pillar of all wisdom, is to know that there is a First Being. Say it once in your head, and notice which word your mind catches on: foundation, pillar, know, or first. Don't explain it; just stay near that one word, and come back to it each time you drift.
Sefer HaMadda. The Book of Knowledge, the opening book of Maimonides' code, where foundations, character, study, idolatry and repentance come before everything else. Today's word.
Your line: knowledge first. Why you do a thing comes before how. See you tomorrow.

1143.title: Foundation of foundations
1143.hook: the code opens with knowing that there is a first Being
1143.howItsDone: Students of the Mishneh Torah often begin with this opening halakhah, and some learn it by heart in Hebrew. Jews who study Maimonides' code read these chapters as a guide to knowing God through careful thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sefer HaMadda, the Book of Knowledge, which puts knowing before doing. Your line: knowledge first. Today, its very first sentence.

Yesod. In Hebrew, a foundation, the part of a building nobody looks at. Walls get painted. Windows get admired. The foundation sits under the soil, and if it shifts, the whole house cracks. Now double the word. Not a foundation, but the foundation of foundations, the one under all the others. That is how Maimonides opens his entire code of Jewish law: with one sentence about what everything else stands on.
screen: `YESOD: A FOUNDATION.` → `THE ONE UNDER ALL THE OTHERS.` → `THE CODE'S OPENING SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here is the sentence, in plain English: the foundation of foundations and the pillar of wisdom is to know that there is a First Being, and that it brings every other thing into being. First, the verb. Maimonides says to know. Not to feel, not to hope, not simply to accept. For him this is something the mind works at, the way it works at geometry, and the following chapters lead the reader through reasoning, not only through faith. Second, what kind of Being. If you could imagine it did not exist, he goes on, nothing else could exist. Imagine everything else gone, and it alone would still be. Everything leans on it. It leans on nothing. Third, the commandment. Knowing this, he says, is a commandment, and he points to the opening words of the Ten Commandments: "I am the LORD thy God." For him, that line is the first thing the Torah asks a person to know. Last week, Crescas asked whether belief in God can be commanded at all. Here is the view he was answering. Fourth, a detail some readers love. In Hebrew the opening runs yesod ha-yesodot ve-amud ha-chochmot. Take the first letter of each word: yud, heh, vav, heh. Together they spell the name of God written with those letters. Some see a signature hidden in the cornerstone. Others call it a lovely coincidence. Either way, the code's first sentence carries the name inside it.
screen: `TO KNOW, NOT ONLY TO FEEL.` · `EVERYTHING LEANS ON IT.` · `I AM THE LORD THY GOD.` · `THE NAME HIDDEN IN THE FIRST LETTERS.` · then, large: `FOUNDATION OF FOUNDATIONS.`

segments.voice: Feel what's holding you up: the chair, the floor under the chair, the building under the floor, the earth under the building. Let your attention go down layer by layer, and notice that you didn't build any of it, and it holds you anyway. If you pray, rest with the words "I am the LORD thy God"; if you don't, simply stay with the feeling of being held from below.

Your line: foundation of foundations. Everything else in the code stands on that one sentence. Go gently.

1144.title: Love and awe (Yesodei HaTorah 2:2)
1144.hook: contemplating the wonders of creation leads to love and awe
1144.howItsDone: Jews who study Maimonides read Yesodei HaTorah 2:2 as a guide to the commandments to love and to fear God, and some take it as a reason to study the natural world as part of a religious life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the code's first sentence: know there is a First Being, the one everything leans on. Your line: foundation of foundations. Today, a feeling the Torah commands.

The Torah commands love: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart." It also commands awe, or fear. But a feeling is a strange thing to command. Nobody can be ordered into loving someone. So Maimonides asks, right there in his code, in the second chapter: what is the way to love God, and to stand in awe? His answer doesn't begin with a prayer or a rule. It begins with looking at the world.
screen: `THE TORAH COMMANDS LOVE.` → `CAN A FEELING BE COMMANDED?` → `HIS ANSWER: LOOK.`

segments.voice: Love and awe. In Hebrew, ahavah and yirah. His answer, in plain English: when a person thinks carefully about God's great and wondrous works and creatures, and sees in them a wisdom with no measure and no end, that person at once loves, and praises, and longs to know. First, the road in. Love doesn't come from willpower. It comes from attention. Look closely at how a thing is made, and something in you moves toward its maker. The person thirsts, he says, borrowing from the Psalms: "My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God." Second, the turn. Keep looking, and the same thoughts bring you up short. You step back, a small creature with a little knowledge, before a wisdom without limit. That is awe, and again he reaches for a psalm: "What is man, that Thou art mindful of him?" Third, the pairing. One act of attention produces both. Love draws you closer. Awe makes you step back. He holds them together, like breathing in and breathing out. Fourth, what comes next. His code goes on to describe the world as the science of his day understood it: the spheres, the stars, the elements. Some of that science has not lasted. The method has: learn how the world works, and let what you learn lead to wonder. For Maimonides, studying creation isn't a distraction from the religious life. It's one of its doors.
screen: `AHAVAH AND YIRAH.` · `ATTENTION LEADS TO LOVE.` · `THEN YOU STEP BACK: AWE.` · `ONE LOOK, TWO MOVEMENTS.` · then, large: `MY SOUL THIRSTETH FOR GOD.`

segments.voice: Look closely at one natural thing, a leaf, a stone, your own hand, as if you'd never seen one before: its edges, its lines, how it's put together. Notice if something moves toward it, a little warmth, a little delight. Then notice the other movement, the step back before how much you don't know, and let both be there.

1145.title: Laws of character
1145.hook: diet, sleep, speech and health are spiritual practice
1145.howItsDone: Some Jews study Hilkhot De'ot as practical guidance for daily habits, and Jews who keep the tradition say blessings before and after eating, turning ordinary meals into moments of attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahavah and yirah: look closely at creation, and love and awe both follow. Your line: love and awe. Today, the same book turns to dinner.

Early in a book about knowing God, the subject changes. Suddenly there's advice about when to eat. Don't eat unless you're hungry. Don't drink unless you're thirsty. Don't fill your stomach all the way; stop while there's still some room. Advice about sleep. Advice about how much to talk. It sits in the Book of Knowledge, not far from the foundation of foundations, written in the same voice as the laws about God.
screen: `A BOOK ABOUT KNOWING GOD.` → `THEN: WHEN TO EAT.` → `SAME BOOK, SAME VOICE.`

segments.voice: De'ot. Usually translated character: the settled habits of a person's temper. Hilkhot De'ot, the laws of character. Earlier this block we heard Maimonides on the middle way. Today he takes it into the body. First, the reason. Keeping the body healthy and whole, he says, is part of the ways of God, because a sick person can't understand or know the Creator. A body in pain pulls the mind away. Caring for it isn't vanity. It's clearing the road. Second, the details. Eat when hungry. Stop about a quarter short of full. Don't eat in a rush. Sleep enough, and at night. He even writes about exercise before meals. A law code that reads, in places, like a doctor's note. Third, the intention. A person should eat, drink, sleep and work with one aim, he says: a healthy body, so the soul can serve God. Someone who lives that way serves God all the time, even while sleeping, because the rest is taken in order to serve. Sleep becomes a kind of worship, not for what happens during it, but for why. Fourth, speech. Speak about wisdom and kindness. Say less. Behind his advice sits the old teaching from Pirkei Avot: silence is a fence for wisdom. Diet, sleep, speech, health. Ordinary days, with a reason running underneath.
screen: `DE'OT: SETTLED HABITS OF CHARACTER.` · `A HEALTHY BODY CLEARS THE ROAD.` · `EAT, SLEEP, WORK FOR ONE AIM.` · `SAY LESS.` · then, large: `THE BODY SERVES THE SOUL.`

1146.title: The physician
1146.hook: court physician in Cairo, he advised moderation in everything
1146.howItsDone: Jewish tradition honors medicine as a calling, and Jewish law expects a sick person to seek a doctor's care; some Jews read Maimonides' medical advice alongside his laws of character.

segments.voice: Yesterday, De'ot, the laws of character, and your line: the body serves the soul. Today, the man who wrote them, at work.

A courtyard full of people, waiting. Some are Jews, some are not. Some are officials, some are ordinary people. They're all waiting for one tired man to ride home. Maimonides describes the scene himself, in a letter to Samuel ibn Tibbon, the man translating his work. He goes up to Cairo early in the day to attend the ruler's household, and comes back to find his house surrounded by patients. He barely eats before he starts seeing them, and he keeps going into the night.
screen: `A COURTYARD FULL OF PATIENTS.` → `A LETTER TO HIS TRANSLATOR.` → `CAIRO BY DAY, PATIENTS BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The physician. In Hebrew, rofe. First, the job. The man who wrote a code of all Jewish law and a philosophical guide also earned his living by medicine, serving at the court and treating ordinary people at home. Scholar and doctor, the same person on the same day. Second, the advice. His medical writings keep returning to an idea we've met in his ethics: moderation. Not too much food, not too little. Exercise, but don't exhaust yourself. Sleep in its season. And he watches the mind as well as the body: worry, grief and anger, he warns, take a toll on health, and a settled, cheerful spirit helps a person heal. Third, the link. His law code gives a doctor's advice about meals and sleep. His medical advice turns to the temper of the mind. The same measure runs through both. For him, medicine and ethics are one way of thinking, applied twice. Fourth, the healer behind the healer. The Torah has God say, "for I am the LORD that healeth thee." A doctor who believes that doesn't stop practicing medicine. Maimonides worked, prescribed and wrote. Caring for the body and trusting God were not rivals for him. The tired man in the courtyard does both at once, patient by patient, until the lamps are lit.
screen: `SCHOLAR AND DOCTOR, SAME DAY.` · `MODERATION IN EVERYTHING.` · `ONE MEASURE FOR BODY AND MIND.` · `I AM THE LORD THAT HEALETH THEE.` · then, large: `MODERATION.`

1147.title: Everyone studies
1147.hook: every Jew must study, rich or poor, healthy or sick, young or old
1147.howItsDone: Jewish tradition encourages fixed times for Torah study, alone, with a study partner, or in a class at synagogue, and some Jews follow a daily study cycle so that a little is learned every day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the physician: Maimonides at work, prescribing moderation for body and mind. Your line: moderation. Today, a law with no easy way out.

Who is excused? Surely the person too poor to spare an hour from finding bread. Surely the one who is sick. Surely the old man whose strength is gone, or the father with a family to feed. Maimonides goes down the list, one by one, in his laws of Torah study, and his answer to each of them is the same. Not excused.
screen: `WHO IS EXCUSED?` → `THE POOR? THE SICK? THE OLD?` → `NOT EXCUSED.`

segments.voice: Everyone studies. The law, in plain English: every man of Israel is obligated to study Torah, poor or rich, healthy or suffering, young or very old and weak. Even a poor man who lives on charity and goes door to door. Even a man with a wife and children. He must set a fixed time to study, by day and by night, because the verse says: "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." First, the list. Maimonides names exactly the people anyone would excuse, and doesn't excuse them. Study is not a hobby for people with spare time. Second, the fixed time. He doesn't ask for hours. He asks for a set time, kept. A little, on purpose, regularly. Third, the examples. Among the great sages of Israel, he says, were woodcutters and water carriers, and some were blind, and still they studied day and night. Fourth, how long. Until the day of death. Learning has no graduation. Now, honestly: Maimonides writes this as a duty of men. A little later he says a woman who studies Torah receives reward, but he doesn't make it her obligation, and he adds cautions. Jewish communities read this differently today. Some keep the obligation as he framed it, while also teaching women Torah seriously; others hold women and men to the same duty to learn. Across those differences, the core still lands: being too busy, too poor or too old is not the end of learning.

1148.title: Eight rungs of giving (Matanot Aniyim 10)
1148.hook: from giving grudgingly up to making someone self-sufficient
1148.howItsDone: Maimonides' ladder of tzedakah is taught in Jewish schools and synagogues as a guide to how to give, not only how much.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the law that no one is too busy, poor or old to learn. Your line: everyone studies. Today, the end of a week, and a ladder.

Someone asks for help, and you give. Fine. But how? With a sigh, eyes on your phone, handing over less than you could? Before they even had to ask? Or in a way that means they'll never need to ask again? Maimonides, in his laws of gifts to the poor, says giving isn't one act. It's a ladder: there are eight levels in giving, he says, each one higher than the one below. You met this ladder in your first weeks on the path. Today, every rung.
screen: `YOU GAVE. BUT HOW?` → `GIVING IS A LADDER.` → `EIGHT LEVELS, EACH ONE HIGHER.`

segments.voice: Eight rungs of giving. Climb from the bottom. Lowest: giving grudgingly, with a sour face. Still giving. Still a rung. Next: giving less than you should, but gladly. Then: giving the right amount, but only after being asked. Then: giving before being asked, straight into the person's hand. So far, both people know each other. Now the ladder turns to who knows what. Next: the poor person knows who gave, but the giver doesn't know who received. Some sages, Maimonides says, tied coins into the backs of their cloaks, and the poor came and took them. Higher: the giver knows, the receiver doesn't. Some sages slipped coins secretly through a poor person's door. Higher still: neither knows the other. And at the very top: strengthening a person before they fall, with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so they won't need to ask anyone. The next two days climb those top rungs slowly. Notice the shape. The bottom rungs are about the giver's heart, the middle about the receiver's dignity, the top about the receiver's future. And even the lowest rung is on the ladder. The point isn't to shame anyone at the bottom. It's to show there's always one rung higher. This week walked from the foundation of foundations, through love and awe, the body, the doctor and the student, to the open hand. Knowledge first, and then it turns outward.
screen: `GRUDGING, THEN GLAD.` · `BEFORE THEY HAVE TO ASK.` · `WHO KNOWS WHO GAVE?` · `SO THEY NEED NO ONE.` · then, large: `EACH RUNG HIGHER THAN THE LAST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the last time you gave something, money, time, a favor, and ask honestly, and kindly, which rung it was on. Then picture the same gift one rung up: given more gladly, or before being asked, or more quietly, so the other person keeps their dignity.
Eight rungs of giving. Maimonides' ladder of tzedakah, from the grudging gift at the bottom to helping someone stand on their own at the top. Today's word.
Your line: the eight rungs. Wherever you stand, there's one rung higher. A full week of Maimonides, done.
